mappings.note: Asks for BOTH zero-work conditions (no displacement, force perpendicular) plus an example - the full direction/displacement content of the work definition, LO-1. Still definitional, so not LO-2.

Refutes a sign error about the goalkeeper: force opposes displacement, so the work is negative. Decided from the definition (LO-1), not from any energy change, which is why LO-3 is not cited even though the ball stops.

Contrasts a wall (zero displacement) with a wheelchair (real displacement) and asks for the scientific reason - a direct application of the definition, LO-1. The figure only sets the two scenarios; no data is read, so no LO-71.
Explains the work-energy theorem (LO-3) and, in doing so, has to say what energy IS - capacity to do work - which is LO-4. The paired V54 item only states the theorem, so it carries LO-3 alone.
Defines kinetic energy and states its dependence on m and v squared - the define-KE clause of LO-5. Not LO-6: the relationship is described, never evaluated for a case.

The DERIVATION of 1/2 mv^2 is named in LO-5, and it proceeds by equating the work done to the energy gained, i.e. the work-energy theorem (LO-3). This is what separates it from S84, which only defines KE.

The graded explanation is PE converting to KE (LO-7); the potential energy is elastic rather than gravitational, which is the only respect in which LO-7's free-fall parenthetical does not fit. C8.1 because a labelled diagram is a required deliverable.

The v-squared factor-of-four result worked through the formula - using the expression, so LO-6. Shares its outcome with MCQ O14, which asks the identical thing in one line; the frame offers nothing that distinguishes them.

The stem names the conservation of mechanical energy explicitly (C-2.6-LO-1), the explanation runs on the PE/KE exchange between extreme and mean positions (LO-7), and a labelled diagram is required (C8.1). The MCQ pendulum items ask only where each form peaks, so they stop at LO-7.
Contrasts the CAUSE of kinetic versus potential energy with an example of each - definitional, so LO-5. No conversion between them is traced, which is what would have pulled it to LO-7.
Concept, expression and variables of gravitational PE - the define-and-derive-PE clause of LO-5. LO-6 is withheld because no mass or height is supplied to substitute.
Parts (a) and (b) define and derive mgh (LO-5); part (c) substitutes 5 kg and 10 m into it (LO-6). The item spans both sibling outcomes, which is exactly why both are cited rather than one.
Part (a) is the definition of power and the watt (C-2.6-LO-1); part (b) is a pump power computation (C-2.6-LO-2). Both halves of the power strand in one item.

Part (a) identifies and describes the inclined plane (LO-3); parts (b) and (c) are the MA formula and a numerical MA plus effort, which only C2.6 covers because the frame has no mechanical-advantage outcome.

Part (a) asks for the STATEMENT of the conservation law (C-2.6-LO-1) and part (b) proves it for a freely falling body, which is LO-7's named case. The statement half is what distinguishes this from the many mechanism-only free-fall items.

POOR FIT. Definition of mechanical advantage, its formula and the meaning of MA greater than 1 - three demands, none of which any learning outcome in curriculum 82 states. Only the competency C2.6 names mechanical advantage at all.

Describes what a fixed pulley does and why direction-changing alone is useful - LO-3 - with C8.1 for the required labelled diagram. C2.6 is deliberately absent: the whole point is that this machine gives NO force advantage.

The long version of the winding-road item, and the stem adds 'and work': besides the inclined plane (LO-3) and its mechanical advantage (C2.6), the student must argue that the work against gravity is unchanged, which is LO-1. That extra demand is what separates it from the 2-mark version.
Names and describes the fulcrum, load and effort of a lever - identification of a simple machine and its parts, LO-3. No ratio is formed, so C2.6 stays out, unlike the effort-arm items.

PARTIAL FIT. Classifying levers into Class I and Class II goes beyond LO-3, which only asks that a lever be identified; the frame has no outcome for lever classes. LO-3 is the nearest legal code and no ratio is computed, so C2.6 is not added.

Two demands: why a small effort lifts a big load, which is mechanical advantage (C2.6 only), and the distance trade-off, which follows from the work/energy total being unchanged (C-2.6-LO-1). The lever is given, so no LO-3.

POOR FIT on the efficiency half. The frictionless-ideal argument is conservation of energy (C-2.6-LO-1) and C2.6 carries the machine, but EFFICIENCY - work output over work input - has no outcome anywhere in curriculum 82.

Doubling the ramp length doubles MA = L/h, a pure mechanical-advantage result that only C2.6 can hold; C8.1 for the required diagram of the block on the plane. LO-3 is not cited because the inclined plane is given, not identified.
Skidding truck: the KE is not destroyed but converted to heat and sound, so the conservation law (C-2.6-LO-1) plus the naming of the thermal form (LO-5). Not LO-7 - nothing here is a PE/KE exchange.

Traces a multi-stage chain of energy forms through a watermill (LO-5), whose first link is the water's gravitational PE becoming KE as it descends (LO-7). LO-5 leads because the answer is graded on the whole chain, not the fall.
